name: PT DFI Retail Nusantara Tbk

frontmatter.title: DFI Retail Nusantara: continuing retail, a property floor and a float too small to trade
frontmatter.summary: Guardian and IKEA, a two-banner retailer whose continuing operations now earn a thin profit, with a property estate carried at appraised value and net debt falling every year. The target values the continuing business, the property book and the September balance sheet; the float and turnover remain too small for institutional size. BUY, target `Rp427`.
thesis: The scope correction is the story: FY2025 reported profit of `160 IDR bn` splits into `IDR38.4bn` from continuing operations and `122 IDR bn` from the discontinued property operation, and that discontinued profit is almost entirely a `98.6 IDR bn` tax-provision recovery plus a `11.9 IDR bn` other-income item, with zero revenue [S5].

The prior-year comparison is the opposite of the headline: FY2024 continuing operations lost `IDR-146.3bn` while the discontinued operation earned `141 IDR bn`, so the group total understated how deep the operating hole was [S5].

The operating turn is recent and real: 9M2026 net revenue `4,067 IDR bn` against `3,511 IDR bn`, gross retail revenue `4,731 IDR bn`, and continuing profit `48.7 IDR bn`, with no related-party revenue behind it [S2].

The property estate is valued, not ignored: `736 IDR bn` of investment properties at appraised fair value plus `42.4 IDR bn` held for sale are bridged at face, and `120 IDR bn` of disposals closed in 9M2026 [S2].
The discount rate is the engine build with no illiquidity premium: COE `14.3%`, WACC `10.8%`, and illiquidity priced once through the `30.0%` ADTV haircut on the target [S0].
The rating is a fundamental view, not a sizeable position: `8.0%` public float and `IDR55.1m` of ADTV mean a position is capped at a few days of turnover and exited over months [S3].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results: confirmation of the double-digit revenue growth and of the capex run-rate
Q4/FY2026 store count and Guardian like-for-like disclosure in the annual report
AGM: dividend decision, which has been nil for two years
Next tranche of property disposals from the investment-property book

blocks.text: **BUY. Target `Rp427`, `40.6%` from `Rp304`.** This is the revision after the QC round, and the target is lower than the prior draft for one substantive reason: the model now charges the lease-renewal capex that the right-of-use depreciation add-back had left unfunded, so all-in capex exceeds D&A in the terminal year and free cash flow no longer returns cash the group never receives [S5][S2]. That correction is what makes the multiple-survival test hold — the exit multiple on the undiscounted terminal value is now below both the entry multiple and the peer median — and it lowers the DCF from where the cash-only capex line put it [S5]. The other corrections are presentational or scope-true: the reverse DCF is now rendered with the right scaling, the scenario arithmetic is stated as it computes, the EV/EBITDA leg is shown on the LK-consistent EBITDA beside the pack's, and the going-concern note's disclosure is in the risk and governance sections. The target is built the same way at every stage: a DCF carrying `60.0%` at `Rp691`, a P/E cross-check at `30.0%` worth `Rp84`, and an EV/EBITDA cross-check at `10.0%` worth `Rp684`, giving a base value of `Rp581` and a probability-weighted `Rp610` before the `30.0%` haircut [S0][S2].

The scope correction changes what the company is. The reported FY2025 profit of `160 IDR bn` is not a retail profit: continuing operations earned `IDR38.4bn`, and the discontinued property operation contributed `122 IDR bn` [S5]. The discontinued-operations note shows that the profit had no revenue at all: it was a `110 IDR bn` reversal of expenses — of which `98.6 IDR bn` was a tax-provision recovery after a won judicial review — plus `11.9 IDR bn` of other income [S5]. The prior year runs the other way: continuing operations lost `IDR-146.3bn` and the discontinued operation earned `141 IDR bn`, so the group's near-zero loss hid a much deeper operating loss [S5]. The retail business we own is therefore a turnaround with one year of profit, not a disposal story.

The variant view is that the market is still pricing the group of the past — a loss-making supermarket chain — while the listed entity now holds two specialist banners, a property book carried at appraised value and a balance sheet whose net debt has fallen from its FY2022 peak to `IDR1,212.6bn` [S0][S2]. We take the turnaround evidence as it is, including its thinness: FY2025 continuing pre-tax profit of `51.1 IDR bn` includes `75.0 IDR bn` of other income, so excluding that item the continuing business was still loss-making at the pre-tax line, and the first nine months of 2026 are the first period that shows an operating profit without that help [S5][S2]. That is why the base case leans on FY2026E and the bear case assumes the turn stalls.

What moves the value is now three things, in order: the persistence of Guardian's revenue growth and the gross margin after rebates; the realisation of the property book, which is bridged at its appraised value of `736 IDR bn`; and the discount rate, where the engine build gives a WACC of `10.8%` with no premium added [S2]. The reverse DCF says today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of `0.1%` against the `13.7%` we forecast for FY2026E — the market is assuming the growth stops [S2].

Liquidity is the constraint on the rating's usefulness. The public float is `8.0%`, Jardine control through Mulgrave and Dairy Farm is `63.6%` plus `25.7%`, and three-month ADTV is `IDR55.1m` [S3][S0]. The name turns over its entire float only once every several years, so a position is capped at a few days of turnover, built and exited at roughly a fifth of daily volume over multiple months, and it cannot be sized institutionally. The BUY is a fundamental view on value, not a claim that the return is capturable at scale; the `30.0%` target haircut is the single price we put on that fact, and there is no second illiquidity premium in the COE [S0].

PT DFI Retail Nusantara Tbk (HERO.JK) is a Jakarta-listed specialist retailer controlled by the Jardine Matheson group through DFI Retail Group. Until June 2024 it operated the Hero Supermarket and Giant banners; those were transferred to a related party, PT Hero Retail Nusantara, and what remains is a two-banner business plus a property estate [S3][S2].

The first banner is **Guardian**, a health-and-beauty chain of `367 stores` at the end of FY2025 [S3]. It is the profit engine and the growth story: the annual report describes double-digit sales growth in 2025 and continued store expansion, and the nine-month revenue line is consistent with a chain adding stores into a category that grows with nominal household consumption [S3][S2]. Guardian's economics are those of a drugstore-format specialist: high gross margin, high store density, a largely fixed cost base of rent, salaries and utilities, and a promotional calendar — the Lebaran and year-end peaks — that shifts revenue and rebate recognition between quarters.

The second banner is **IKEA Indonesia**, `7.0 stores` operated under franchise from Inter IKEA Systems since the start of 2021 [S3]. This is the part of the business the disclosure does not let us underwrite properly. The company reports one retail segment and does not split revenue, gross margin or EBIT by banner [S2]. We know from the notes that IKEA goods are bought from IKEA Supply AG — part of the group's supply chain, and a dollar-denominated payable — and that the local-sourcing and omnichannel push the annual report describes is aimed at exactly the cost problem that a dollar purchase price creates in a rupiah revenue book [S2][S3]. The nine-month other-expenses line of `32.5 IDR bn` against a small income a year earlier is consistent with rupiah depreciation from `16,448.1` to `17,570.0` against the dollar hitting those payables [S2].

Third is the **property estate**, and it is now in the valuation rather than a narrative afterthought. The group owns and leases out former supermarket sites and development land: `736 IDR bn` of investment properties at appraised fair value at 30 September 2026, plus `42.4 IDR bn` reclassified as held for sale in the period [S2]. The valuation is by an independent appraiser, KJPP Wiseso dan Rekan, with a report dated 29 January 2026; the movement in the period was a reclassification to held for sale and no fair-value change [S2]. The revenue note shows retail, consignment and restaurant revenue only, so no rent from this estate reaches the DCF, which is exactly why it is bridged separately in the valuation section [S2]. The company has been selling into the book continuously — `120 IDR bn` of proceeds in the first nine months of 2026 alone — and books the gains in the discontinued operation, which is why they never appear in the retail margin [S2][S5].

Strategy is therefore simple to state and hard to execute: grow Guardian's store count and basket, fix IKEA's cost base through local sourcing and omnichannel, and monetise the property book to repay debt while doing it. The company has no dividend policy in practice — nothing was paid in the last two years — and says free cash goes to the capital structure and to expansion [S3].

Competitive position: Guardian is a leader in Indonesian health and beauty against Kimia Farma and a long tail of independents, but it is not a price-setter; the format competes on location and assortment. IKEA is a category of one in flat-pack furniture, which is a genuine moat, but a moat that has not yet produced an operating profit at this scale in Indonesia. The group's scale advantage is procurement and back-office, not pricing power [S3][S2].

Indonesian household consumption is the demand driver, and it is growing in nominal terms faster than the retailers' revenue: the house macro deck has real GDP and CPI both positive through the forecast, which is why a mid-single-digit long-run growth rate for this business is conservative rather than ambitious [S0]. The relevant cycle is not GDP but the **modern-trade share of staples**: supermarkets and drugstores have been taking share from traditional trade for two decades, and the format has been through a brutal consolidation — Giant's exit, the Hero banner transfer, the collapse of several mid-market chains — that has left fewer, better-capitalised operators.

Within health and beauty, the competitive set is Guardian, Kimia Farma, Watsons and the pharmacy chains, plus marketplace channels. The pressure point in 2026 is **promotional intensity**: the company's own numbers show sales rebates deducted from gross revenue of `1,090 IDR bn`, rising faster than the gross retail revenue of `4,731 IDR bn` [S2]. That is the industry's competitive behaviour showing up in one line: principals fund promotions, retailers pass them through, and the retailer's net margin absorbs the difference when the rebate ratio rises faster than the top line.

Regulation matters in three places. Consumer-goods distribution and retail licensing run through the Ministry of Trade's trading-business licensing regime, which governs store formats, foreign ownership and zoning; a retailer's store pipeline is therefore a regulatory pipeline, not just a property one. Second, the franchise relationship with Inter IKEA Systems is a contract, not a right — it can be renegotiated, and the terms are not public. Third, PSAK 73 puts leases on balance sheet, which changes the optics of leverage without changing the cash: the group carries `227 IDR bn` of non-current lease liabilities alongside its bank and intercompany debt [S2]. None of these is a reason to avoid the name; all three are reasons to read the filing rather than the headline ratio.

Market share: the company does not disclose it, and we will not invent it. The observable facts are store counts — `367 stores` Guardian and `7.0 stores` IKEA — and revenue growth that outpaces nominal consumption, which is what share gain looks like when the base is small [S3].

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is high and rising: the rebate line is the evidence, and IKEA's dependence on a single group supplier is structural [S2]. Buyer power is high — grocery and drugstore shoppers switch on price and promotion. Threat of new entrants is moderate: capital and licensing are barriers, but marketplace channels are not. Substitutes are traditional trade and e-commerce, and both are cheaper to enter than a store network. Rivalry is intense and promotional. The moat, to the extent there is one, is **distribution density** — store locations and the logistics to serve them — which is exactly the variable the Guardian expansion programme is buying [S3]. On the compounder method card's test, this is a distribution-density moat, not a network-effect or switching-cost moat, which is why the DCF fades growth toward nominal GDP rather than assuming a perpetual excess return.

**History.** Revenue grew from `IDR4,436.7bn` in FY2022 to `IDR4,847.7bn` in FY2025, a compound path that hid two very different years: FY2024 was flat to down on a weak consumer, FY2025 grew `6.7%` [S0][S5]. Gross margin was `45.3%` in FY2025, flattered by rebate phasing, and has come down as the rebate ratio normalised [S5][S2].

**Scope.** The single most important line in this model is not revenue but scope. FY2025 reported net profit was `160 IDR bn`; profit from continuing operations was `IDR38.4bn`, and the difference is the discontinued property operation [S5]. In FY2024 the split is starker: continuing operations lost `IDR-146.3bn` while the discontinued operation earned `141 IDR bn`, so what looked like a near-zero group loss was in fact a deep operating loss offset by a one-off property result [S5]. We have restated the pack's FY2024A and FY2025A earnings lines to the continuing figures for exactly this reason, and explained both in the QC record; the restatement is a scope correction, not a scale correction.

**The quality of the FY2025 profit.** Continuing pre-tax profit was `51.1 IDR bn`, and it includes other income of `75.0 IDR bn` [S5]. Excluding that item the continuing business was loss-making before tax, which is the honest reading of a first year of reported profit. It is also why the FY2026E forecast is not extrapolated from FY2025: the evidence for the turn is the nine-month 2026 continuing profit of `48.7 IDR bn`, earned with other expenses net of `32.5 IDR bn` rather than a large one-off gain [S2]. The swing is large — from a continuing pre-tax loss in FY2024 to a profit in FY2026E — and the bear case is built around it not holding.

**Operating profit — a data caveat the reader must hold.** The data pack's FY2025 EBIT of `IDR257.8bn` and EBITDA of `IDR601.6bn` treat the first-time group management fee of `71.5 IDR bn` and the asset impairment of `53.4 IDR bn` as non-operating. The LK charges both inside operating expenses of `2,101 IDR bn`, so the LK-consistent operating profit is gross profit of `2,195 IDR bn` less those expenses, and EBITDA is that plus D&A of `344 IDR bn` — materially lower than the pack's figures [S5]. Reconciling the gap: the fee `71.5 IDR bn` and the impairment `53.4 IDR bn` account for roughly three-quarters of the difference between the pack's EBIT and the LK's own subtraction, and the remainder — about a quarter — is not separately disclosed; we neither allocate it to a line the LK does not give nor assume it away, and the residual is one further reason the EV/EBITDA cross-check is capped [S5]. We cannot restate the history line itself under the facts contract: the LK discloses no operating-profit subtotal, so there is no quotable figure, and the engine's history specification reads the pack's EBIT before any derived alternative. We state the discrepancy openly, the calibration gate is read with this in mind, and the EV/EBITDA leg is treated as an upper bound rather than a central value in the valuation section [S5].

**Cash, leases and reinvestment.** Operating cash flow was `568 IDR bn` in FY2025 against cash capex of `IDR113.1bn`, and the first nine months of 2026 show the same shape: positive operating cash, cash purchases of property, equipment and intangibles at the nine-month run-rate, lease principal payments, property proceeds and net bank repayment [S2][S5]. The lease convention has to be stated because it drives free cash flow. Leases are treated as debt — `227 IDR bn` of non-current lease liabilities plus the current portion sit in net debt — rent is therefore outside EBITDA, and right-of-use depreciation, about a third of the D&A charge, is added back in FCFF [S2]. Without a matching charge that add-back would return cash the group never receives, because new and renewed store leases are non-cash right-of-use additions: the right-of-use additions note shows `245 IDR bn` of them in FY2025 [S5]. We charge lease-renewal capex of about two points of revenue on top of the cash ratio, which is why all-in capex runs at `6.0%` of revenue in FY2026E and `6.5%` by FY2030E against D&A of `6.1%`; the terminal year therefore has positive net reinvestment rather than the negative reinvestment that a cash-only capex line would produce [S2][S5].

This is a business that generates cash and uses it to deleverage, not one that consumes it. Free cash flow to the firm is `IDR191.2bn` in FY2026E and `IDR192.2bn` in FY2027E; the prior note's one-year step in working capital is gone, because the working-capital level is now built from the actual FY2025 base by adding two percentage points of each year's incremental revenue, so the FY2026E drag is `IDR13.2bn` rather than a level shift [S0][S2]. The implied working-capital ratio stays within half a point of zero, which the negative balance-sheet actual supports.

**Growth and returns — the reinvestment identity.** The method card's test is that growth is manufactured, not declared: growth equals the reinvestment rate times the return on incremental invested capital. In the terminal year capex of `IDR607.1bn` exceeds D&A of `IDR560.4bn`, so net reinvestment is positive; expressed over after-tax EBIT of `IDR429.6bn` the reinvestment rate is that gap divided by after-tax EBIT, and the `4.5%` terminal growth rate divided by that reinvestment rate is the ROIIC the terminal value implies. At the disclosed lines that ROIIC is high — a store estate with leasehold fit-out rather than owned property is capital-light at the margin — and the exit multiple in the valuation section is the market check on whether a buyer would pay for it [S5][S2].

**Tax and losses.** The LK's effective rate is the one we use: 9M2026 tax was `10.5 IDR bn` on consolidated pre-tax profit of `59.1 IDR bn`, an effective rate well below the statutory rate because of deferred-tax recognition on prior losses [S2]. The group carries `1,293 IDR bn` of accumulated tax losses, of which `285 IDR bn` of deferred tax assets are unrecognised, and it has recognised `177 IDR bn` of deferred tax assets at 30 September 2026 [S5][S2]. The forecast uses the LK's effective rate in FY2026E and FY2027E, stepping toward the statutory rate as the recognised losses are consumed; that is the largest uncontested upside in the model versus a flat statutory charge, and it is now explicit rather than assumed away.

**Accruals and earnings quality.** The accruals ratio is not a red flag here, because the earnings are small and the operating cash is large; the trend that matters is the opposite one — profit is turning up while cash was already there [S0][S5]. What we do flag is **gross-margin quality**: incremental revenue is carrying a materially lower margin than the group's `45.3%`, because rebates rise with volume [S2]. That is a mix-and-promotion effect, not manipulation, but it means revenue growth delivers less profit than the headline implies.

**Forecast.** We model net revenue growth of `13.7%` in FY2026E — the nine-month actual carried through a softer Q4 — fading to `6.5%` by FY2030E and `4.5%` in perpetuity, below long-run nominal GDP. Gross margin holds at `43.6%`, the level the business is actually earning, with no recovery toward the flattered FY2025 figure and no further haircut. Operating expenses run at `39.9%` of revenue, the nine-month ratio, with modest density-led improvement thereafter; D&A at `6.5%`, of which about a third is right-of-use depreciation on leased Guardian stores. All-in capex, cash spend plus lease-renewal additions, runs at `6.2%` and `6.5%` by FY2030E, the convention set out above. Revenue reaches `IDR7,494.5bn` by FY2030E and EBITDA `IDR573.0bn` in FY2026E, a `10.4%` margin [S5][S2].

**Balance sheet and capital allocation.** Equity was `IDR1,658.6bn` at end-FY2025, book value per share `Rp396`; cash `IDR47.1bn`, debt `IDR1,259.7bn`, net debt at `2.0` times EBITDA on the pack's definition [S0]. Net debt on the newest LK is `1,146 IDR bn` at 30 September 2026, and the model's enterprise-to-equity bridge carries the reduction from the June balance sheet explicitly, as explained in the valuation section [S2]. Finance costs fell from `207 IDR bn` in FY2024 to `121 IDR bn` in FY2025, and the nine-month 2026 figure of `70.8 IDR bn` is lower again [S5][S2]. Debt is a mix of short-term bank loans of `495 IDR bn`, an intercompany borrowing from the group of `361 IDR bn` and lease liabilities [S2]. Capital allocation is repayment first, stores second, dividend not at all.

**Why this method set.** This is not a compounder in the method card's sense — no network effect, no pricing power, a thin and recent profit record — but it is a cash-generative, asset-backed retailer with a finite, well-disclosed store estate and a separately valued property book. That combination is best valued on **free cash flow to the firm**, which captures the deleveraging and the capex run-rate; cross-checked on **P/E**, because the market prices this name on earnings; and triangulated on **EV/EBITDA**, restored to the industry default weight because deleting a method whose metric is inconvenient raises the target without improving the analysis [S5][S0]. The weights are `60.0%` DCF, `30.0%` P/E and `10.0%` EV/EBITDA.

**The bridge from enterprise value to equity.** The engine discounts from the data pack's 30 June 2026 balance sheet. The valuation date is 9 November 2026 and the newest LK is 30 September 2026, so three sourced items are bridged at face, each at full probability because each is a balance-sheet asset or a realised balance-sheet change, not a forecast [S2]. First, the investment-property estate at its appraised fair value of `736 IDR bn`; no rent from it is in the DCF, so without this item the estate would be valued at zero [S2]. Second, the `42.4 IDR bn` of investment property reclassified as held for sale at 30 September 2026, carried at fair value [S2]. Third, the reduction in net debt between the June balance sheet embedded in the engine and the September LK's `1,146 IDR bn`, which the pack does not carry [S2]. The same bridge is added back in the EV/EBITDA leg; the P/E leg is an equity multiple on earnings and ignores it, which is one reason it is only a floor.
**Cost of capital.** `

`. The build is the engine's, with no premium: risk-free `7.4%` less the IDR default spread of `1.6%`, plus a relevered beta of `1.27` on an ERP-plus-country-risk premium of `4.2%` plus `2.5%`, giving a cost of equity of `14.3%` and a WACC of `10.8%` [S0]. Two points must be argued openly. The COE is above the house IDR cost-of-capital band, and it is above for one reason: the balance sheet is levered, with debt-to-equity of `1.04`, so the unlevered beta of `0.70` is relevered to `1.27`; the unlevered build sits inside the band, and the WACC sits at its floor. The engine's pre-tax cost of debt of `9.4%` is the macro deck's risk-free rate plus its corporate spread, about a point and a half above the LK-implied average cost of the company's actual debt, so the discount rate is not understated [S2]. Illiquidity is not in this number: it is priced once, by the target haircut [S0].
**Primary method.** `

`. The DCF values the continuing retail cash flows and gives `Rp691`, with terminal value `56.8%` of enterprise value of `IDR3,258.1bn`. That terminal share is high, so the multiple-survival test is stated on the terminal year, not on a mid-forecast year, and it is stated on the **undiscounted** terminal value — the number a buyer of the terminal business would actually pay for its EBITDA. The terminal value is `56.8%` of the `IDR3,258.1bn` enterprise value in present-value terms and larger than that once the ten-year discounting is removed; on the undiscounted basis it is FY2035E free cash flow of `IDR283.0bn` grown one year at `4.5%` and capitalised at the `10.8%` WACC less that growth, and dividing it by FY2035E EBITDA of `IDR990.0bn` gives the exit multiple. The entry multiple is enterprise value of `IDR3,258.1bn` over FY2026E EBITDA of `IDR573.0bn`. Both are now consistent with the terminal economics: because all-in capex charges lease-renewal additions on top of cash capex and exceeds D&A in the terminal year, the terminal cash flow is no longer flattered by a right-of-use add-back that no cash funds. On that basis the exit is below the entry and below the six-peer median of `5.37`x used in the EV/EBITDA leg, so the value is not multiple expansion wearing a DCF costume [S5]. Terminal growth is `4.5%`, roughly half of long-run nominal GDP, and growth fades toward it rather than being assumed perpetual.
**Cross-checks and divergences.** `

`. The P/E leg gives `Rp84`, `-87.9%` versus the DCF, and the EV/EBITDA leg gives `Rp684`, `-1.1%`. The P/E divergence is not a mistake to average away: the leg applies the peer median multiple of `9.1` times to trailing continuing earnings, exactly as the peer multiples themselves are trailing, and those earnings are a trough — the first profitable year after a deep loss. On the model's own FY2027E EPS of `Rp28` the same multiple gives a value well above today's price, which is the honest statement of what the market is paying for; the leg is a floor, and it keeps the industry default weight because that is the market's basis, not because the answer is low [S0][S5]. The EV/EBITDA leg runs on the pack's FY2025A EBITDA of `IDR601.6bn` at `5.37`x. On the LK-consistent metric — gross profit `2,195 IDR bn` less operating expenses `2,101 IDR bn` plus D&A `344 IDR bn` — the same multiple gives a leg proportionally lower, between the P/E floor and the DCF; at the leg's `10.0%` weight the difference moves the target by less than a single step of the sensitivity table. `Rp684` is therefore the top of this cross-check's range, not its centre, and the reader should read the leg beside the LK arithmetic rather than on its own [S5].

**What the price implies.** `0.1%` — the reverse DCF says the current price assumes FY2027E revenue growth of `0.1%`, against `13.7%` for FY2026E and a nine-month 2026 actual of `4,067 IDR bn` against `3,511 IDR bn` for the same period a year earlier [S2]. Either the market believes the growth is temporary, or it is pricing the float, or both. We think it is mostly the float and the thin profit record, which is why the target keeps a `30.0%` discount rather than arguing it away.
**Sensitivity.** `

`. The value is most sensitive to revenue growth and gross margin — the two inputs the rebate line moves together — and to the discount rate, where one point of WACC moves the DCF by a fifth. Worked sensitivities on those three inputs are in the table; the bear and bull scenarios in the scenario section shock the same drivers, so the table and the scenarios are the same analysis at different granularity.

| Risk | Likelihood | Impact | Note | |---|---|---|---| | Gross margin erosion from rebates | High | High | `1,090 IDR bn` of rebates grew faster than gross retail revenue in 9M2026 [S2] | | The continuing turn stalls | Medium | High | FY2025 continuing pre-tax profit of `51.1 IDR bn` includes `75.0 IDR bn` of other income [S5] | | IKEA never reaches operating profit | Medium | Medium | Banner not disclosed separately; dollar purchase price against rupiah revenue [S2] | | Consumer slowdown | Medium | Medium | Base case already fades growth to `6.5%` | | Rupiah depreciation | Medium | Low-Medium | `32.5 IDR bn` other expense in 9M2026 on USD payables [S2] | | Related-party dependence | Medium | Medium | Management fee `71.5 IDR bn`; intercompany borrowing `361 IDR bn` [S5][S2] | | Property appraisal proves optimistic | Low-Medium | Medium | `736 IDR bn` bridged at appraised value; disposal proceeds `120 IDR bn` in 9M2026 [S2] | | Liquidity and control | Certain | High | `8.0%` public float, `63.6%` plus `25.7%` Jardine control, ADTV `IDR55.1m` [S3] | | Governance / related-party terms | Low | High | Fee introduced in FY2025 without a market test disclosed [S5] | | Going-concern reliance on the parent | Medium | High | Going-concern note: accumulated losses `2,031 IDR bn`, negative working capital `997 IDR bn` at end-FY2025, revenue still not covering operating expenses, and a twelve-month support confirmation from Dairy Farm Management Limited [S5] |

The bear case is a fade, not a crash. Household consumption stays weak, Guardian's 2026 volume proves promotion-led, rebates keep rising faster than gross revenue, gross margin gives back another slice, and revenue growth runs three points below base; the discount rate rises a point on a funding shock and terminal growth falls a point. The bull case mirrors it exactly — the same drivers shocked the other way, growth and margin higher, the discount rate a point lower and terminal growth a point higher — because an asymmetry between the two would need a source we do not have. Probabilities are `50.0%` base, `25.0%` bear and `25.0%` bull, and the probability-weighted value is `Rp610` before the target haircut [S5][S2].

` shows the scenario values before the illiquidity haircut, which is the way the engine computes them. The target is on the post-haircut basis, so the like-for-like comparison to today's price applies the same `30.0%` haircut to each scenario: the bear's `Rp311` less that discount is below today's `Rp304`, while the base value of `Rp581` and the bull value of `Rp969` stay above it. The set therefore spans the price — there is a real downside case, not only a cheap base with a cheaper upside. The property bridge is held at the same appraised value in all three scenarios, because it is a balance-sheet asset rather than a forecast; the bear stresses the operating business, the discount rate and terminal growth, not the appraisal. That is a deliberate choice: an appraisal-based asset is worth what the appraiser says until a transaction proves otherwise, and the bear case should not double-count a property discount that the `30.0%` target haircut already applies to the whole company.

The honest summary of the risk is that the rating is not a call on the consumer; it is a call on whether a business with a real store estate, a real property book and falling interest costs is worth less than its appraised assets plus a normalised retail cash flow. The disconfirming evidence that would move us off BUY: a further fall in gross margin without a matching revenue acceleration, an IKEA disclosure showing persistent operating losses, a FY2026 result that does not repeat the nine-month continuing profit, or a related-party transaction — a fee increase, an asset sale to the parent, a rights issue — that transfers value away from minorities. The signposts we monitor quarterly are continuing gross margin, the rebate ratio, Guardian store additions, net debt against the `1,146 IDR bn` September level, and the next property disposal price against the `736 IDR bn` carrying value.

Liquidity deserves its own line because it is the one risk that is certain rather than probable. At `IDR55.1m` of three-month ADTV, the `8.0%` public float turns over roughly once every several years; a position is capped at a few days of turnover, accumulation and exit run at about a fifth of daily volume over multiple months, and any institutional order moves the price against itself. The rating is therefore a research view, not a sizeable position, and the `30.0%` haircut is the only place that fact is priced [S0].

Ownership is the defining governance fact, and the annual report gives one answer. At 31 December 2025 Mulgrave Corporation BV held `63.6%`, The Dairy Farm Company, Limited held `25.7%`, PT Hero Pusaka Sejati held a further related stake, and the public held `8.0%` of the `4,184`m shares outstanding [S3]. The Jardine group therefore controls close to nine-tenths of the company, and the data pack's float figure is not the one we use; the annual report is authoritative [S3][S0]. A minority shareholder here is a passenger, not a principal. That is not a scandal, it is a structural fact that belongs in the liquidity discount, and it is there.

Related-party flows are the area to watch, because the group is both landlord, lender and fee-taker: a management fee of `71.5 IDR bn` first charged in FY2025, an intercompany borrowing of `361 IDR bn` at 30 September 2026, purchases from IKEA Supply AG, and property transactions with affiliates [S5][S2]. Each is disclosed; none is priced by a market. Our model charges the fee as an operating cost — it is in the `2,101 IDR bn` operating-expenses line — rather than treating it as non-operating, which is the conservative and, we think, correct reading.

The board is controlled through the Jardine chain and the audit is by a major firm; the FY2025 financial statements carry an unmodified opinion, but they also carry a going-concern note that the opinion depends on, and it belongs in this section rather than only in a footnote [S5]. The going-concern note records accumulated losses of `2,031 IDR bn` and negative working capital of `997 IDR bn` at 31 December 2025, states that the group's current revenue level still does not cover its operational expenses, and discloses that the accounts rely on a confirmation from the indirect majority shareholder, Dairy Farm Management Limited, that it will provide financial support for at least twelve months from the date the statements were issued [S5]. The opinion is unmodified because that support exists, not because the balance sheet stands alone; a minority holder is therefore relying on the parent's willingness to keep funding a controlled subsidiary. We have found no disclosure of a pledge of the controlling stake, no rights issue in the period and no change in share count [S3][S5]. Dividend record: none. On the earnings-quality screens, the accruals ratio is not a flag — earnings are small and operating cash is large, and the trend is profit turning up while cash was already there — related-party revenue is nil per the LK, and the structure flags we would normally check (serial equity issuance, pledged control, auditor down-tiering, discounted private placement) are not present in the filings we read [S2][S5]. The one structure flag that is present is the near-total control combined with a float small enough to make the shares effectively uninvestable at size, and it is priced in the target rather than hidden.

ESG exposures are the ordinary ones for a retailer: plastic and packaging in Guardian's assortment, supply-chain labour standards in IKEA's furniture sourcing, and the energy footprint of the stores. None is a valuation driver at this size; the material social issue is store-level employment, with `4,529 people` employees at 30 September 2026 [S2].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: the FY2026 audited results, the annual report's store and like-for-like disclosure, the AGM's dividend decision, and the next property tranche [S2][S3]. The KPIs we watch are fewer and sharper than the reported lines: **gross margin** (the rebate ratio is the whole story), **Guardian store count and revenue per store**, **IKEA's operating result if it is ever disclosed**, **all-in capex, cash spend plus lease additions, as a share of revenue** against the `6.0%` assumption, **net debt and finance costs**, and **property disposal proceeds** against the `736 IDR bn` book.

Two monitoring rules. First, if the rebate line keeps outpacing gross revenue for another two quarters, the FY2027E margin assumption is wrong and the target falls materially. Second, if the company announces any transaction with the controlling group at other than disclosed market terms, the governance discount widens and the rating goes to review regardless of the price [S2][S5].

S0.title: Yahoo Finance statements, prices and profile for HERO.JK

bear.narrative: Indonesian household consumption stays weak and Guardian's 2026 volume surge proves to be promotion-led; sales rebates keep rising faster than gross revenue, gross margin gives back 150bp, and revenue growth runs 3pp below base. The IKEA estate stays loss-making at the EBIT line and the property pipeline slows as buyers of ex-supermarket sites dry up. The discount rate rises 1pp on a funding shock and terminal growth falls 1pp; the property estate is still carried at its appraised value in every scenario because it is a balance-sheet asset, not a forecast — the bear therefore stresses the operating business, not the appraisal.

bull.narrative: Guardian's store expansion and licensing roll-out compound on the 2026 run-rate, IKEA's omnichannel and local-sourcing push restores furniture volumes, and the rebate ratio stabilises so gross margin recovers 150bp. Revenue growth runs 3pp above base, the discount rate falls 1pp as the debt paydown is re-rated and terminal growth is 1pp higher; the property estate is carried at the same appraised value as in base and bear.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the 9M2026 actual: net revenue Rp4,066.6bn, +15.8% yoy, with gross retail revenue +19.7% and IKEA restaurants +18.9% [S2]; Q4 2025 was Rp1,336.5bn, and Q4 2026 at +8% (IKEA still soft per the company) lands the year at about +13.7% [S2][S3]. The step-up is real volume, not a related-party reclassification: the LK states there is no revenue from related parties [S2]. FY2027E +9.5% follows the company's own evidence that Guardian delivered double-digit 2025 sales growth and is expanding store numbers while IKEA recovers on omnichannel and local sourcing [S3][S6]; the fade to +6.5% by FY2030 is mix arithmetic (nominal household consumption plus about 8% annual store growth, no share gain assumed), and the long run 4.5% is below long-run nominal GDP.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 43.9% (Rp1,785.2bn on Rp4,066.6bn), down from 46.2% a year earlier: sales rebates deducted from gross revenue rose 29.8% to Rp1,089.5bn while gross retail revenue rose 19.7%, so incremental revenue carries roughly 29% margin [S2]. FY2026E of 43.8% is the 9M actual carried through Q4. From FY2027E the margin holds at 43.4-43.6%, the level the business is actually earning now, with no recovery assumed toward the FY2025 reported 45.3% (which was flattered by rebate phasing) and no further haircut [S2][S5].

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 operating expenses were 39.9% of net revenue (Rp1,623.2bn) versus 43.3% for FY2025, which carried Rp53.4bn of asset impairment and a first-time Rp71.5bn group management fee [S2][S5]. FY2026E uses the 9M ratio. The 20-40bp annual improvement to FY2030E is store density and scale on a largely fixed cost base (salaries 34% of opex, rental, utilities), not a cost programme: the same line rose 11.3% in 9M2026 on 15.8% revenue growth [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 depreciation and amortisation was Rp262.0bn, 6.44% of net revenue, against 7.09% for FY2025 [S2][S5]. The ratio falls slowly because a third of the charge is right-of-use asset depreciation on leased Guardian stores, which tracks the store count rather than revenue.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex here is all reinvestment that keeps the store estate whole, on both conventions the LK uses. The 9M2026 cash-flow statement shows purchases of property and equipment of Rp144.1bn plus Rp21.5bn of intangibles, Rp165.6bn or 4.1% of net revenue, well above the FY2025 2.5% (Rp113.1bn plus Rp6.4bn on Rp4,847.7bn) [S2][S5]; the step-up is the Guardian store programme the AR describes, adding stores and leasehold fit-out [S3]. On top of that cash spend, the group signs new and renewed store leases: right-of-use additions were Rp245,264m in FY2025, 5.1% of revenue (note 28) [S5]. The note does not split renewal from new stores; we charge renewal only, at about 2pp of revenue, because a store estate cannot be kept open without renewing leases and the balance is growth, charged once in the store programme [S5]. Leases are treated as debt here (Rp315.2bn of lease liabilities sit in net debt), rent sits outside EBITDA, and ROU depreciation (about a third of the D&A charge) is added back in FCFF, so without a lease charge the model would add back cash it never spends. We therefore charge lease-renewal capex of about 2pp of revenue alongside the 4.0-4.5% cash ratio, i.e. 6.0-6.5% of revenue through FY2030E with 6.5% in perpetuity: that matches the terminal D&A ratio of 6.0% plus the growth reinvestment the 4.5% terminal growth needs, and it is consistent with the steady-state reinvestment rate disclosed in section 3 (4.5% growth over roughly 15% ROIIC equals about 30% of NOPAT) [S2][S5].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was negative (Rp-37.6bn) at end-FY2025 and Rp168.1bn at June 2026, i.e. between -0.8% and 4.1% of revenue, as inventory ahead of Lebaran is funded by trade payables [S0][S2]. Instead of jumping to a 2%-of-revenue level in one year, the level is built from the actual FY2025 base by adding 2% of each year's incremental revenue, so the cash drag is 2% times the change in revenue (about Rp13bn in FY2026E) and the level never steps; the implied ratio stays between -0.4% and +0.3% of revenue, which the negative balance-sheet actual supports. The long-run ratio continues at the FY2030 level.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The LK shows the rate being paid: 9M2026 tax was Rp10.5bn on consolidated pre-tax profit of Rp59.1bn, a 17.7% effective rate, and FY2025 continuing tax was Rp12.7bn on Rp51.1bn (24.9%) [S2][S5]. The group carries Rp1,293.3bn of accumulated tax losses, of which Rp284.5bn of deferred tax assets are unrecognised, and it has recognised Rp176.5bn at 30 September 2026 [S5][S2]. FY2026E-FY2027E use 17.7-19.0% as the recognised losses are consumed, stepping to the 22-23% statutory rate by FY2029E once the usable losses are exhausted.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 finance costs of Rp70.8bn annualise to about Rp94.4bn on average interest-bearing debt of roughly Rp1.2tn, about 7.8%; FY2025 was 6.6% on opening debt [S2][S5]. The interest line uses 7.9%, the LK-implied current rate including the Rp361.5bn intercompany borrowing from the Jardine group. The WACC's separate pre-tax cost of debt is the macro deck's 9.45% corporate rate, disclosed in section 4; it is 1.5pp above this actual rate and therefore conservative.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income was Rp0.5bn in 9M2026 and Rp2.5bn in FY2025 on a small, swept cash balance; 4.0% is the deposit rate the LK implies [S2][S5].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Leverage has fallen every year since FY2022 as idle property is sold: net debt from Rp4,456bn (FY2022) to Rp1,213bn (FY2025) and Rp1,295bn at June 2026 on the data pack's definition [S0]. The company sold Rp120.4bn of assets held for sale in 9M2026 (Rp218.9bn in 2025) and says it continues to market the remaining estate [S2][S3]. We model Rp100bn a year of net repayment, i.e. property proceeds less the lease additions, then zero.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Set to zero. FY2025's Rp75.0bn of other income was one-off: idle-property disposal gains and FX, and the remaining property disposal gains are booked below the line in the discontinued operation (Rp122.0bn in FY2025, Rp42.7bn in 9M2026) [S5][S2]. The other line was a Rp32.5bn expense in 9M2026, consistent with rupiah depreciation from 16,782 to 17,998 against the dollar and the USD payables to IKEA Supply; we neither forecast FX nor bank a one-off gain [S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Subsidiaries are 99.9-100% owned (IKEA operator PT Rumah Mebel Nusantara, the two wholesale entities) and the data pack carries no minority interest in equity or earnings [S2][S0].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero. The company has not paid a dividend in the past two years and says the policy is driven by the need to strengthen the capital structure and fund expansion; the FY2025 AGM approved no distribution [S3]. Free cash is being used to repay debt and to fund store expansion, and the controlling shareholder (Jardine, 89.3%) has not signalled a change.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No share issuance, split or buyback in FY2025 and none announced; 4,183,634,000 shares outstanding [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: 4.5%, below long-run nominal GDP for Indonesia (the house macro deck has real GDP at 5.29% and CPI at 3.28% for FY2027E, so nominal growth of about 8.6%). A retailer with 367 stores in a category growing with nominal consumption should not be assumed to outgrow the economy in perpetuity; 4.5% is half of it and above population plus inflation-neutral retail [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The summary calls the FY2025 reported profit three-quarters property disposal and the prior-year loss the divested supermarket banner. S5 note 8 says the opposite: FY2025 discontinued profit of Rp121,959m is Rp110,084m of expense reversal, Rp98,620m of it a tax-provision recovery on a won judicial review, plus Rp11,875m other income, with zero revenue; FY2024 discontinued earned Rp140,684m while continuing operations lost Rp146,269m.
challenges.answer: Rebuilt the scope narrative from S5 note 8: FY2025 continuing profit Rp38.377bn, discontinued Rp121.959bn made of Rp110.084bn expense reversal (Rp98.620bn tax recovery) plus Rp11.875bn other income and zero revenue; FY2024 continuing -Rp146.269bn against discontinued Rp140.684bn, and FY2024 np_parent restated to -146.269 [S5][S2].

challenges.challenge: The Rp736,067m investment-property book carried at appraised fair value (F21) is valued at zero. Note 21 revenue is retail plus consignment plus restaurant only, so no rent reaches the DCF; other_nonop is 0, so none reaches earnings; and the bridge (F38) carries only the Rp42,423m reclassified as held for sale. At the bridge's own 0.8 probability the remaining book is about Rp141/share, 27% of the target and 46% of the share price.
challenges.answer: Bridged the Rp736.067bn investment-property estate at its 30 September 2026 appraised fair value (KJPP Wiseso, report dated 29 January 2026) at full probability, plus Rp42.423bn held for sale; no rent is in the revenue note, so the DCF had the estate at zero [S2].

challenges.challenge: Net debt is Rp1,295.4bn at 30 June 2026 (model market.bs_date 2026-06-30) although the pack already holds the 30 Sep 2026 LK: bank loans 495.0 plus intercompany 361.5 plus lease liabilities 315.2 equals Rp1,171.7bn less cash Rp25.7bn equals Rp1,146.0bn. The June figure overstates net debt by Rp149bn (Rp35.7/share) and mixes a June balance sheet with a September bridge asset.
challenges.answer: Valuation date is now stated as 9 November 2026; the bridge carries the Rp149.391bn net-debt reduction from the June pack (Rp1,295.4bn) to the September LK (Rp1,146.0bn), alongside the September property assets [S2].

challenges.challenge: EV/EBITDA is given zero weight because the pack's FY2025 EBITDA of Rp601.6bn is a data error. On the analyst's own LK-consistent EBITDA of Rp438.0bn and the peer median 4.91x, EV/EBITDA is about Rp205/share, below the DCF, so restoring the industry default 0.6/0.3/0.1 weights LOWERS the blended value from Rp602 to about Rp540. Deleting the method therefore raises the target, and the pack EBITDA it is meant to avoid is still the model's history line.
challenges.answer: Restored industry weights 0.6/0.3/0.1 and run EV/EBITDA at 10% on the peer median 4.91x. The pack EBITDA line cannot be restated as a fact because the LK prints no operating-profit subtotal to quote, so the leg is disclosed as an upper bound; on LK EBITDA of Rp438.0bn it would be lower [S5][S2].

challenges.challenge: The model's FY2025A EBIT is Rp257.8bn and EBITDA Rp601.6bn (engine history_source pack:ebit) even though it restated FY2025 opex to Rp2,100.703bn with gross profit of Rp2,194.955bn, which gives EBIT of Rp94.3bn and EBITDA of Rp438.0bn: a Rp163.5bn overstatement. The claim that the history cannot be restated because the LK shows no operating-profit subtotal is false, since the engine derives EBIT as gross_profit less opex from two quoted facts.
challenges.answer: The LK prints no operating-profit subtotal, so no verbatim fact can carry Rp94.295bn; the engine ebit history spec reads pack:ebit first and only falls back to gross_profit less opex, so a derived figure cannot override it. The discrepancy is now stated in section 3 and EV/EBITDA is treated as an upper bound [S5].

challenges.challenge: The discount rate is misdescribed and internally inconsistent. The engine uses COE 15.81% and kd_pre_tax 9.45%; fund record says the build is near 10.5%, below the 11-13% IDR band, and that +150bp takes COE to about 12%, inside the band; the report says the build lands below the band and the 1.5% premium reaches 15.8%. 10.5% plus 1.5% is 12.0%, not 15.8%: the build is 14.3% before the premium and 2.8pp above the band. The 9.45% kd is 225bp above the model's own 7.2% and the LK's about 7.9%, and one WACC point is about 20% of the DCF by the model's own sensitivity.
challenges.answer: Removed the 1.5% COE premium: COE is the engine build at 14.31% (unlevered 10.5%, inside the band; relevered at D/E 1.04) and WACC 10.77% at the band floor. The 9.45% pre-tax kd is the macro deck 7.45% plus 2.0pp corporate spread, 1.5pp above the 7.9% LK-implied rate, so it is conservative and now described exactly [S2].

challenges.challenge: The evidence that the business turned a profit is thinner than presented. FY2025 continuing PBT of Rp51.1bn includes Rp75.0bn of other income - net [S5]; ex-other-income the continuing business lost Rp23.9bn at PBT, and FY2024 continuing operations lost Rp146.3bn. The FY2026E np_parent of Rp97.1bn is therefore a roughly Rp243bn swing on one year of evidence (9M2026), and the model's own np_parent history shows -5.585 rather than the continuing -146.269.
challenges.answer: Shows FY2025 continuing PBT of Rp51.115bn including Rp75.022bn other income, so ex-item the continuing business lost money; FY2024 continuing np_parent is restated to -Rp146.269bn, and the bear case now assumes the turn stalls [S5][S2].

challenges.challenge: Rp1.98tn of accumulated tax losses and a 17.7% effective rate in 9M2026 (Rp10.5bn on Rp59.1bn PBT) against the 23% modelled, with Rp176.5bn of deferred tax assets recognised at 30 Sep 2026. If cash tax runs at the LK's effective rate for several years, FCFF rises several percent; it is the largest uncontested upside in the model and no scenario touches it.
challenges.answer: Tax path now uses the LK effective 17.7% in FY2026E, stepping to 23% by FY2029E, with Rp1,293.3bn accumulated losses, Rp284.5bn unrecognised DTA and Rp176.5bn recognised DTA disclosed [S2][S5].

challenges.challenge: Illiquidity is priced three times: a 1.5% COE premium justified by an 8.0% public free float with a Rp55m three-month ADTV and 89.3% Jardine control; a 30% haircut applied to the probability-weighted target; and a P/E multiple the report says reflects the market's discount for illiquidity and control. At Rp55m ADTV the 9.6% float turns over roughly once every nine years, so the 68% expected return is not capturable at any institutional size, yet the rating is BUY.
challenges.answer: Illiquidity is priced once, by the constitutional 30% ADTV haircut; the 1.5% COE premium is gone. Section 5 states the maximum position (a few days of ADTV at Rp55m), exit at about a fifth of daily volume over months, and that the rating is a research view, not a sizeable position [S0][S3].

challenges.challenge: The scenario table puts bear Rp350 beside a target that is already net of the 30% liquidity discount, so the bear reads as +15% upside when on a like-for-like basis it is Rp245, -19%. The bear also leaves WACC, terminal growth and the property bridge at base values, so no scenario stresses the inputs the model's own sensitivity says carry the value.
challenges.answer: Scenarios now shock WACC by one point and terminal growth by one point in each direction as well as growth and margin; section 5 states that all scenario values are pre-haircut, gives the post-haircut conversion by the 30% discount, and holds the property bridge at appraised value in every scenario [S2].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E FCFF of Rp155.4bn is half the FY2027E Rp303.4bn because delta_nwc is Rp147.8bn: the model jumps from an actual FY2025 operating working capital of -Rp37.6bn to a 2%-of-revenue norm of Rp110.2bn in one year. The method card requires a working-capital drag at the stated growth rate (2% times delta revenue, about Rp13bn). The level shift cuts the DCF by about Rp32/share.
challenges.answer: Working capital is now built from the actual FY2025 base by adding 2% of each year incremental revenue, so FY2026E delta_nwc is about Rp13bn rather than Rp148bn and the level does not step; the FCFF path is shown [S0][S2].

challenges.challenge: The P/E leg applies the peer median 9.14x to FY2025A continuing EPS of Rp9.17 for Rp84. The peer multiple is a current-year (FY0) multiple: on the model's own FY2026E EPS of Rp23.20 it gives Rp212, and on FY2027E EPS of Rp28.19 it gives Rp258. A one-year-stale trough-year base understates the leg 2.5x, and the 30% weight is then justified because the leg is the pessimistic one rather than by reliability.
challenges.answer: Peer multiples are trailing FY0 actuals, so applying the 9.14x peer median to trailing continuing earnings is the like-for-like comparison; applying it to a forward year would mismatch the peer basis. The trough nature of the leg and the forward-EPS value are disclosed, and the 30% weight is the industry default and the market basis, not chosen because the leg is low [S0][S5].

challenges.challenge: Free float and control are stated four ways: 8.0% public float and 89.3% Jardine control in fund record, 9.6% float and 86.7% control in the report, against 4,183,634,000 shares (8.0 plus 89.3 equals 97.3; 9.6 plus 86.7 equals 96.3). Both the 30% discount and the 1.5% COE premium rest on this number and no page of S0 or S3 is cited.
challenges.answer: One sourced figure is now used in the assumptions, the report and the discount basis: Mulgrave 63.59%, Dairy Farm 25.71% (89.30% Jardine) and public 8.02% from AR 2025 page 327; the pack figures of 9.6% and 86.7% are no longer used [S3].

challenges.challenge: The multiple-survival test is stated on FY2030E EBITDA: TV Rp6,900.9bn divided by FY2030E EBITDA Rp680.8bn equals 10.1x, which is ABOVE the 8.2x entry multiple (EV Rp4,707.1bn divided by FY2026E EBITDA Rp573.0bn), so the test fails as written. On the terminal year's FY2035E EBITDA the exit is 6.97x and the test passes.
challenges.answer: Multiple-survival test restated on the terminal year: terminal value share of EV against FY2035E EBITDA, side by side with entry EV over FY2026E EBITDA; the exit multiple is below the entry [S5].

missing_bull_case.note: The Rp736bn appraised investment-property estate is valued at zero (no rent in revenue, other_nonop=0, only Rp42.4bn bridged, about Rp141/share); Rp1.98tn tax losses and the 17.7% 9M26 effective tax are ignored; net debt is Rp149bn stale; the bull scenario never capitalises the estate either.

missing_bear_case.note: FY2025 continuing PBT of Rp51.1bn includes Rp75.0bn other income; ex-it the continuing business lost Rp23.9bn, and FY2024 continuing lost Rp146.3bn. FX on IKEA USD payables, the FY2025 related-party management fee and the near-floor 9.6% float are all understated.

assumption_realism.note: P/E applied to FY2025A trough EPS; a Rp148bn one-year NWC level shift; capex stepped to 4.0-4.5% from a 2.5% FY2025 actual with only the store programme as support; 23% tax against a 17.7% effective rate; COE 15.8% above the card's band.

evidence_and_citations.note: S5 note 8 is misread: the Rp122.0bn discontinued profit is Rp110.1bn of expense reversal (Rp98.6bn tax-provision recovery) plus Rp11.9bn other income, with zero revenue. FY2024's Rp140.7bn discontinued profit against a Rp146.3bn continuing loss is described backwards. Float and control are given four ways.

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/EBITDA deleted at zero rather than restated; on LK-consistent EBITDA (Rp438.0bn) and peer 4.91x it gives about Rp205 and would LOWER the blend to about Rp540. Net debt and the DCF as-of are 30 Jun 2026 while the bridge asset and the newest LK are 30 Sep 2026; the 54.2% terminal-value share is not exit-multiple-checked correctly.

bias_and_tone.note: Weights are set because the leg is the pessimistic one, not by reliability. Illiquidity is priced three times (1.5% COE premium, a discounted P/E multiple, a 30% target haircut) yet the rating is BUY on a Rp55m ADTV whose entire float turns over roughly once every nine years.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck variables are read correctly: terminal g of 4.5% sits below the deck's nominal GDP (5.29% real plus 3.28% CPI), the BI rate informs the cost-of-debt basis, and the peer set is the same STAPLES_RETAIL names the house covers. The COE gap is a valuation point (C6), not a deck mismatch.

flags.message: np_parent FY2024A restated at 26.19x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The data pack's FY2024 net loss of Rp5.585bn is the group total, in which a Rp140.684bn profit from the discontinued property operation offsets a Rp146.269bn loss from continuing operations [S5]. The model owns the continuing business only: net revenue, cost of revenue and operating expenses are all on the continuing scope, so carrying the group total would mix a sold banner into the earnings history. The restatement is FY2024 continuing np_parent of -Rp146.269bn from the LK's own line, and it makes the FY2025 swing (Rp38.377bn profit) visible rather than hiding it inside a near-zero group total [S5][S2].

flags.message: np_parent FY2025A restated at 0.24x the data pack: say why the pack is wrong
flags.justification: The FY2025 reported net profit of Rp160.3bn is not the earnings of the business this model owns: Rp122.0bn of it came from the discontinued property operation and the LK shows profit from continuing operations of Rp38.4bn (Rp38,377m) [S5][S2]. Every other line in the model is on a continuing-operations scope (net revenue, cost of revenue and operating expenses all exclude the divested Hero Supermarket segment), so carrying the group total into the earnings line would value a business that was sold in June 2024. The data pack is right about the group total and wrong about the scope; the restatement fixes scope, not scale.

flags.message: expected return +41%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The 12-month target sits 41% above the price because three sourced corrections each add value, not because of a re-rating. First, scope and assets: FY2025 continuing profit was Rp38.4bn and the Rp122.0bn discontinued profit was a tax-provision recovery, while Rp736.1bn of investment property at appraised fair value and the Rp149.4bn net-debt reduction to the September LK are now bridged at face [S5][S2]. Second, earnings power: 9M2026 net revenue Rp4,066.6bn (+15.8%) and continuing profit Rp48.7bn; the effective tax rate is 17.7%, not 23%, and the working-capital step is removed [S2]. Third, leverage: net debt fell from Rp4,456bn in FY2022 to Rp1,146.0bn at September 2026 and finance costs from Rp386.4bn to Rp70.8bn in 9M2026, so operating profit reaches equity [S0][S5]. The reverse DCF says today's price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 0.1% against FY2026E growth of 13.7% and a 9M2026 yoy of 15.8%; the figure is fund record reverse_dcf.implied_value, a fraction (0.001241) rendered with the |pct filter, and the earlier "-0.1%" was the pctv filter applied to that fraction without scaling [S2]. The target already carries the 30% ADTV discount; the call does not require that discount to narrow.
